title: Describe the Painting
statement: Each segment [start, end, color] paints the half-open interval [start, end) with a distinct color number. Overlapping paint mixes by adding colors. Return the painting as non-overlapping pieces [start, end, mixedSum], ordered left to right, omitting unpainted parts. A new piece begins wherever the set of colors changes (so two neighbouring pieces may have equal sums).

large_tests.gen_code:
import random
def gen():
    r = random.Random(30)
    segs = []
    for i in range(20000):
        a = r.randint(0, 99000)
        segs.append([a, a + r.randint(1, 1000), 2 * i + 1])
    return [segs]

hints.1_question: Between any two consecutive 'interesting' coordinates (where some segment starts or ends) the mixed color does not change. What are the interesting coordinates?
hints.2_nudge: Record +color at each start and -color at each end in a dictionary. Walk the coordinates in sorted order keeping a running sum.
hints.3_big_hint: For consecutive sorted coordinates prev, x: if the running sum before x is > 0, emit [prev, x, sum]. Then add diff[x] to the sum. Do not merge neighbours; colors differ even if sums match.

known_bugs.name: merges neighbouring pieces with equal sums
known_bugs.followup: Two neighbouring pieces have the same total. Are they made of the same set of colors? What does the problem say about when a new piece starts?

known_bugs.name: includes unpainted gaps as pieces with sum 0
known_bugs.followup: Should a stretch with no paint appear in the output?

known_bugs.name: sweeps every integer coordinate (O(range * segments))
known_bugs.followup: If coordinates go up to 100000 and there are 20000 segments, how much work is it to test every segment at every coordinate? Which coordinates actually matter?

followups: Why is a dictionary + sorted keys better than an array when coordinates are huge?
Why is it important that all colors are distinct?
